title: Streaming throttle fallbacks and long-history POC - Vela Retail
summary: AE + SE ran an edge-cases POC walkthrough focusing on very long conversation history (~250k tokens), peak TPS bursts, and streaming backpressure. Discussed strategies: incremental KV cache eviction, model fallbacks, chunked streaming with client-side resume, per-route latency SLOs, and telemetry needed for Optimize recommendations. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a 48-hour synthetic stress with Vela prompts, share console dashboards + telemetry spec, and follow up with pricing for Dedicated pool plus canary rollout plan.

streaming backpressure handling and client strategies

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-07 16:00 PST | Duration: 55 min | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Vela), Tasha Nguyen (Vela), Oliver Price (Vela)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Walkthrough of streaming failure modes when sessions are extremely long and TPS spikes. Focus on graceful degradation, fallback to smaller model variants, and client resume strategies.

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro, im Maya, AE on Redwood, and with me is Jordan our SE who will run through the demo. Samir, Tasha, Oliver - thanks for joining, do you want to do quick intros?
[00:00:18] Samir: Yeah hi Samir here, head of ML at Vela, we own the in-app assistant infra. We're basically trying to understand if Redwood can handle our long purchase conversational histories and the flash holiday TPS spikes.
[00:00:28] Tasha: Tasha, platform eng. We care about egress costs and latency p95 under load, and also the on-prem constraints for some EU customers.
[00:00:00] Oliver: Oliver, CTO - mostly here to see risk profile and rollout options.
[00:00:45] Jordan: Cool thanks, I'll jump into the console demo in a minute. Quick call goals: show live behaviour for very long histories (~50-250k token windows), simulate high TPS bursts, and specifically demonstrate streaming backpressure and the fallback controls in Console + Optimize recommendations. Also cover Dedicated / Private options.
[00:01:10] Samir: Sounds good, and we wanted to see how streaming handles mid-response stalls caused by KV-cache misses or when a queue saturates.
[00:01:22] Jordan: Right, we built a few scenarios. I'll start with a live session that has intentionally long context - we stitched several prior conversations into a single conversation so you can see memory blowouts and how prefix/KV caching interacts.
[00:01:38] Jordan: (screen share) ok, this is the session view in Redwood Console — little UI glitch the console shows "KV cash" in the tooltip sometimes, ignore that, it's the KV cache. Here is the session metadata: context length ~180k tokens, pinned model is rw-large-8q, fallback chain set to rw-medium-8q -> rw-small-4q, streaming enabled, clientResume token set.
[00:02:05] Tasha: Wait, 180k tokens? how does the runtime keep that without OOMs?
[00:02:12] Jordan: Good question. behind the scenes we don't keep raw history in GPU memory; we maintain a KV cache for active session tokens and we write cold history to prefix storage. When the active window exceeds a configured threshold, the runtime will evict older KV entries and fallback to the prefix-only path which increases latency for specific tokens but prevents OOMs.
[00:02:35] Samir: So are evicted entries lost for good or can they be re-hydrated on request?
[00:02:40] Jordan: They can be re-hydrated but that's a heavier op; we do on-demand re-warm and you get a latency spike for the chunk that rehydrates. That is where we recommend client-side chunking and resume logic; if a stream stalls, client can request remaining tokens using resumeToken so it's idempotent.
[00:03:01] Tasha: Our mobile clients can't tolerate big spikes though. we'd prefer graceful degradation rather than big stalls.
[00:03:07] Jordan: Exactly - that's why Console has two knobs: aggressive truncation (drop older messages) vs cascade to smaller model variants which have lower memory footprint. For UX-sensitive routes we recommend cascade fallback: keep response streaming but switch to a smaller model that can handle the tail. The transcript might be slightly different in quality but latency stays low.
[00:03:30] Oliver: How does model switching affect token costs? We have a hard budget target.
[00:03:36] Maya: cost tradeoffs: smaller models lower per-token cost but may require more tokens if they hallucinate and you prompt more. Optimize can run sample prompts and recommend per-route quantization and batching so you get a cost curve.
[00:03:51] Samir: Can you show the TPS burst simulation? that's the other big unknown.
[00:03:57] Jordan: Yeah switching to the load sim tab — we're going to replay a 10-second flash where TPS goes from 200 to 2400 and hold for 60s, then back off. Console shows request queue depth, token throughput, and per-model concurrency.
[00:04:15] [00:04:15] Jordan: starting replay in 3,2,1..
[00:04:20] [00:04:20] Console: queue depth rising... latency p95 spikes to 1.3s -> 2.1s -> Then fallback trigger: policy 'latency-first' activated, a subset of requests rerouted to Dedicated burst pool and some to rw-medium-8q variant.
[00:04:45] Samir: hmm i'm seeing intermittent 503s in the sim. are those real or artifact?
[00:04:50] Jordan: In this mode, 503s are coming from our older client keep-alive settings in the simulator. On real traffic we recommend client-level retry with exponential backoff and idempotency keys. Redwood also supports per-route automatic retry + circuit breaker config in Console which we used for this demo.
[00:05:08] Tasha: Can the system backpressure at the transport layer to signal clients to slow down?
[00:05:13] Jordan: Short answer: yes, but depends on your integration. For streaming we send SSE/chunked responses and will pause writes when internal buffers are saturated; clients see stalling and can implement a clientbackoff. We also provide a 429 hint header when queues exceed threshold so smart clients can back off proactively.
[00:05:31] Samir: That 429 hint header would be super useful to avoid retries that just amplify the spike. Does Optimize tune thresholds automatically?
[00:05:38] Jordan: Optimize can recommend thresholds based on historical traces and token distributions if you opt-in to telemetry. It will also suggest batch sizes and quantization profiles per model for cost/latency sweet spots.
[00:05:49] Oliver: Let's talk security for a sec - we have EU customers that require data not leave our VPC.
[00:05:55] Maya: For that you'd want Redwood Private. we can deploy control plane connectors into your VPC and you can use your KMS. Private supports the same fallback and streaming semantics; the only difference is customer-managed networking and optional air-gapped components.
[00:06:10] Tasha: latency-wise that sounds fine, but what about logging? We need audit logs but can't export raw content.
[00:06:17] Jordan: Console supports token-level cost/latency breakdowns and you can redact or hash content before logs leave the VPC. We also support audit log sampling and encrypted storage with customer keys.
[00:06:30] Samir: ok back to the failure modes — what happens to ongoing streams during a node fail?
[00:06:36] Jordan: If a GPU node fails mid-stream, we have per-chunk acknowledgements in the runtime. The client might see a short reconnect; if the request was partially emitted we can resume from the last acked chunk given the resumeToken. Otherwise fallback policies can immediately route to a warm standby model variant to avoid user-facing errors.
[00:06:57] Tasha: Does resumeToken rely on deterministic decoding? if the model is quantized differently can you replay the same token sequence?
[00:07:05] Jordan: Great callout — exact token-for-token resume only guaranteed for the same model + quantization profile. For cross-variant resume we use syntactic checkpoints: we can resume from a recent stable prefix and continue generation; you can expect minor divergence in output but typically acceptable for assistant use-cases.
[00:07:26] Samir: Is there a recommended max session window you'd advise? We think 250k might be near our upper bound for some customers.
[00:07:33] Jordan: We typically recommend designing for a 100-150k active window with cold-prefix archival. Above that you should expect higher chance of reheat spikes. If you absolutely need 250k-active, Dedicated pool with larger GPU types + nvmemory with high-quantization can hold it but cost goes up; Optimize will help quantify that.
[00:07:52] [00:07:52] Jordan: switching to a short failover demo — I'll intentionally saturate KV cache to force eviction and show client resume.
[00:08:05] [00:08:05] Jordan: (typing) send request... streaming response starts... halfway through I trigger eviction...
[00:08:18] [00:08:18] Console log: KV eviction event at t=14s, rewarm op started, latency spike recorded for chunk 2, client sees a 600ms stall then resumes.
[00:08:30] Samir: ok i saw the stall. that 600ms is acceptable sometimes, but our in-product experience expects under 200ms.
[00:08:37] Maya: This is where cascade fallback helps - rather than rewarming (which spikes), route to smaller model with available KV capacity and keep streaming. The content might lose some long-tail context but the UX is maintained.
[00:08:52] Tasha: For analytics, what events should we capture on our side to detect these stalls proactively?
[00:08:58] Jordan: capture: stream chunk latency histogram, resumeToken events, 429 hint count, queue depth at ingress, and model-switch events. Send them as custom metrics or through our ingestion endpoint. Optimize can consume those to recommend batch sizes and KV thresholds.
[00:09:18] Samir: One more thing - how do you test for corner cases? we want to validate before pilot.
[00:09:23] Jordan: We can run synthetic replays of your production traffic — that's what we propose for the POC. For the demo today we've got a synthetic generator that can produce extreme session lengths and burst TPS; we'll run a 48-hour stress as the next step and share dashboards.
[00:09:40] Samir: ok that works. Are there any obvious integration pitfalls?
[00:09:45] Jordan: Common pitfalls: not sending idempotency keys (leads to duplicate generation on retries), client keep-alive too short (triggers false 503), not reading 429 hint headers, and assuming token-level determinism across quantization variants. We provide best-practices in the SDKs and the suffix of the Console shows recommended client settings.
[00:10:05] Tasha: SDK - do you have mobile-friendly libs that handle resume and backoff for us?
[00:10:10] Maya: Yes we have JS/Android/iOS helpers that implement resumeToken handling, exponential backoff, and chunk-level acking. We also support a light-weight webhook mode for async callbacks if you don't want streaming.
[00:10:22] Samir: Can you show the Optimize UI quickly - we want to see batching recommendations?
[00:10:28] Jordan: (screen) Optimize shows a per-route cost/latency frontier. For your assistant route it suggests batch_sizes 8->16 for rw-medium-8q, quantize to 4-bit for rw-small-4q where acceptable, and enable prefix-caching at 60% hit-rate. There's a slider where you can pick your cost vs latency tradeoff and it generates a recommended config.
[00:10:53] Tasha: If we apply that config, what's the risk of quality regressions?
[00:10:57] Jordan: Optimize ties config changes to a set of held-out prompts (you can upload your eval set). It will run A/B evals and show regressions with diffed responses. You can gate rollout on a quality threshold.
[00:11:12] Oliver: Cool. Let's recap the constraints: we need p95 < 300ms for primary flows, cost under $X/token target, and EU traffic not to traverse public internet. We want a pilot inside 2 weeks.
[00:11:25] Maya: Noted. Proposed pilot: Dedicated reserved pool sized for your typical plus 2x peak, run 48h synthetic with Vela prompts, instruments telemetry for Optimize, and then a staged canary (10% -> 50% -> 100%) over 2 weeks. Pricing + SLA sheet I'll share.
[00:11:42] Samir: Sounds good. I have a couple of quick technical clarifications: 1) how long before a rewarm completes? 2) what is default client keep-alive?
[00:11:50] Jordan: rewarm time depends on how many layers need to be materialized; typically 150-800ms for small warmups, several seconds for large. default keep-alive in our SDK is 30s; we recommend 90s for flakier networks.
[00:12:08] Tasha: and fallback policies - can they be per-route? we have different SLAs per route.
[00:12:12] Jordan: Yes, per-route policies. Console shows policy inheritance - global defaults, then per-route overrides. You can define a policy that says: if p95 latency > 400ms for 30s, then route to fallback chain, enable quantization, and send 429 hints to client.
[00:12:29] Samir: ok. Anything about billing when fallback triggers? i.e., if you route to smaller model mid-request how is cost attributed?
[00:12:36] Maya: Billing is token-level by model; the Console reports per-token model attribution and the billing export will show the split across variants. For complex multi-model sequences we provide a trace with per-chunk model ids.
[00:12:49] Oliver: For the POC, we need the shared benchmarks and the telemetry spec.
[00:12:54] Maya: we'll share both, Jordan will run the stress and invite you to the live dashboard.
[00:12:59] [00:12:59] Quick audience crosstalk - (inaudible)
[00:13:05] Samir: small nit - earlier you mentioned 'resumeToken' semantics and deterministic resume only for same quantization. do you have a recommended way to present resumed output to users when the text diverges?
[00:13:16] Jordan: show a 'continuing response' indicator and if needed give a short contiguous summary of the resumed prefix. UX pattern is to mark resumed content and optionally collapse older context.
[00:13:29] Tasha: ok makes sense.
[00:13:32] Jordan: All right, next I'm going to flip to a short chaos run to show multi-region fallback - simulate EU region losing network to public internet and how Private can keep traffic local.
[00:13:41] [00:13:41] (screen) sim starts... EU region isolation triggered... traffic reroutes to Private cluster in FRA, data forwarding disabled, latency metrics stable.
[00:13:58] Samir: that is helpful. are the Private deployments managed by Redwood ops or handed over to us?
[00:14:04] Maya: They are hybrid - we provide the control plane and deployment manifests, but you can opt for fully customer-managed on-prem install if needed. For VPC Private we still run the control plane with tenant-level isolation.
[00:14:16] Oliver: SLA question — can you commit to failover times?
[00:14:20] Maya: For Dedicated we have SLA targets and measurable failover windows; we'll include the exact numbers in the pricing + SLA doc.
[00:14:29] Samir: cool. anything else on the technical side?
[00:14:33] Jordan: Two final items: telemetry schema (we'll share a JSON spec) and a short checklist for SDK integration.
[00:14:41] Tasha: Please send the telemetry spec before the stress run so we can map custom metrics.
[00:14:45] Maya: will do.
[00:14:48] Jordan: ok wrapping up, summary of decisions: Redwood runs 48h synthetic stress using Vela prompts; use Dedicated burst pool for pilot with cascade fallback policy; Vela provides traffic profile and sample prompts; Redwood shares pricing + SLA and telemetry spec.
[00:15:05] Samir: sounds good to me.
[00:15:08] Oliver: good meeting. thanks.
[00:15:12] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invite for the live dashboard watch.
